issues.title: Things to check
issues.empty-input: We couldn't find any directive in this text.
issues.violation-message: This is an error message, not your policy. It only shows the rule that blocked something ({directive}). Find the whole policy, then paste it here.
issues.violation-message-unnamed: This is an error message, not your policy. It only shows the rule that blocked something. Find the whole policy, then paste it here.
issues.unknown-directive: "{directive}" isn't a CSP directive, so browsers ignore it. Is it a typo?
issues.duplicate-directive: "{directive}" appears more than once. Browsers only use the first one and ignore the rest.
issues.deprecated-directive: "{directive}" is deprecated or has no effect in modern browsers.

deprecated.report-uri: "report-uri" is the older way to receive violation reports. It still works, and browsers that don't support report-to yet only report through it: keep it, and add report-to beside it.
deprecated.prefetch-src: "prefetch-src" was removed from the specification and current browsers ignore it. You can delete it.
deprecated.block-all-mixed-content: "block-all-mixed-content" is obsolete: browsers now upgrade or block insecure content on secure pages by themselves. You can delete it.
deprecated.plugin-types: "plugin-types" is obsolete: browsers no longer run plugins such as Flash or Java. You can delete it; object-src 'none' is what still matters.
deprecated.navigate-to: "navigate-to" was dropped from the specification before any browser supported it, so it has no effect. You can delete it.
deprecated.require-sri-for: "require-sri-for" never became a standard and current browsers ignore it. To check that scripts haven't changed, put integrity attributes on the script tags.

issues.ignored-in-meta: "{directive}" is ignored when the policy is set with a <meta> tag. It only works as an HTTP header.
issues.missing-quotes: "{value}" in {directive} should be written with quotes ('{value}'). Without them the browser treats it as a website name.
issues.invalid-source: "{value}" in {directive} isn't a valid value, so browsers ignore it.
issues.none-with-other-sources: {directive} contains 'none' together with other values; 'none' is then ignored.
issues.report-only-in-meta: Report-only policies can't be set with a <meta> tag; browsers ignore this one.
issues.empty-directive: {directive} has no value, which blocks everything of this type.
issues.strict-dynamic-without-nonce: {directive} has 'strict-dynamic' but no nonce or hash, so no script on the page can run. 'strict-dynamic' only trusts the scripts that a nonced or hashed script loads.
issues.placeholder-nonce: '{value}' in {directive} is the builder's placeholder. Your server must replace it with a new random value for every page it sends.
issues.hash-length: The hash '{value}' in {directive} doesn't have the right length, so it never matches any code. Copy it again in full.
issues.ignored-in-report-only: "{directive}" has no effect in a Report-Only policy: browsers ignore it there. Put it in the enforced policy.

simple.introReported: We'd like to use {vendors} on {site}. I checked our Content-Security-Policy (the browser rule that lists which outside services our pages can use): nothing blocks them, but our report-only policy would report them, so they would show up in the violation reports:
simple.needsNonceLine: {vendor}: our policy only trusts scripts carrying a one-time code (nonce). The tool supports it, but the way it is added to the page needs to pass the code on. {how}
simple.reportedLine: {vendor}: our policy is in report-only mode, so nothing is blocked, but these would show up in the violation reports.

risk.unsafe-inline-script: {vendor} asks for 'unsafe-inline' on scripts. It's common for marketing tools but weakens protection against malicious code. If we use (or can use) nonces, that is a safer option: {how}
risk.unsafe-inline-style: 'unsafe-inline' on styles is requested for {vendor}. The risk is limited (it affects how the page looks, not what code runs).
risk.unsafe-eval: {vendor} asks for 'unsafe-eval', which lets the page turn text into code. It is only needed for the feature "{feature}" and could be left out if we don't use it.
risk.wildcard: {source} allows every subdomain of that vendor. This is what {vendor} documents.

intro.simple: If the code written in your pages rarely changes, each block can be approved one by one instead of all at once. Paste them here to get the policy to use.
intro.technical: List each inline block by its `'sha256-…'` hash. Once a hash is in the directive, browsers ignore `'unsafe-inline'` there: it stays only for very old browsers.

warning.script: Every other inline script on your pages stops running until its hash is listed, and so do `onclick="…"` attributes. Test with `Content-Security-Policy-Report-Only` first.
warning.style: Every other `<style>` block on your pages then needs its hash too. Test with `Content-Security-Policy-Report-Only` first.
warning.styleAttr: `style="…"` attributes keep working: `style-src-attr 'unsafe-inline'` is added for them.

trustedTypes.toolsNote: This policy turns on Trusted Types, and the tools picked don't say in their documentation whether they work with it. Where a tool writes HTML or loads scripts, the browser may stop it. Test with `Content-Security-Policy-Report-Only` first. [What Trusted Types change](/trusted-types)

findings.script-unsafe-inline: 'unsafe-inline' in {directive} lets any injected inline script or event handler run, which removes most of the protection against XSS. Nonces or hashes allow your own inline code without it.
findings.script-unsafe-hashes: 'unsafe-hashes' in {directive} allows the inline event handlers whose hashes are listed. Safer than 'unsafe-inline', but those handlers remain; moving them into script files removes the need.
findings.script-unsafe-eval: 'unsafe-eval' in {directive} lets the page turn text into code (eval(), new Function()), so injected data can end up running. Keep it only if a tool you need requires it.
findings.plain-url-schemes: {value} in {directive} allows scripts from any address with that scheme, including a site an attacker controls.
findings.plain-wildcard: {directive} allows '*', any website, so it does little against injected content.

missing-directives.object-src: Plugins (<object>, <embed>) aren't restricted, and they can run JavaScript. Set object-src 'none'.
missing-directives.script-src: Scripts aren't restricted: there is no script-src and no default-src to fall back on. This is the rule that protects against XSS.
missing-directives.base-uri: No base-uri: an injected <base> tag could send every relative script address to an attacker's server, even with nonces. Set base-uri 'none' or 'self'.

script-allowlist-bypass.known: {value} is known to host JSONP endpoints or Angular libraries that let an attacker run code despite this policy. Remove it, or move to nonces with 'strict-dynamic'.
script-allowlist-bypass.unverified: No known bypass on {value}, but if it serves JSONP replies or Angular libraries, an attacker can use it to run code. Host allowlists are hard to keep safe; nonces with 'strict-dynamic' are more robust.
script-allowlist-bypass.self: 'self' trusts every file on your own site. If it hosts JSONP endpoints, Angular or files uploaded by users, they can be used to get around the policy.

object-allowlist-bypass.known: {value} is known to host Flash files that let an attacker get around this policy. Set object-src 'none'.
object-allowlist-bypass.restrict: object-src allows {value}. Plugins are rarely needed today: can it be 'none'?

ip-source.localhost: {directive} allows localhost ({value}). Fine while developing; remove it in production.
ip-source.ip: {value} in {directive} is an IP address rather than a host name. Browsers may not match it, so it may allow nothing; use the host name.

findings.nonce-length: The nonce {value} is shorter than 8 characters and could be guessed. Generate a new random value of at least 128 bits for every response.
findings.nonce-charset: The nonce {value} uses characters outside base64. Use a base64 value.

src-http.resource: {value} in {directive} is loaded over plain HTTP, which anyone on the network can change. Use https://.
src-http.report: Violation reports are sent to {value} over plain HTTP. Use https:// so they can't be read or changed on the way.

findings.deprecated-directive: {directive} is deprecated and modern browsers ignore it.

unknown-directive.colon: Directive names don't end with a colon, so {directive} is ignored.
unknown-directive.unknown: {directive} isn't a CSP directive, so browsers ignore it.

findings.missing-semicolon: {value} in {directive} looks like a directive name, not a value. Is a semicolon missing before it?

invalid-keyword.quotes: {value} in {directive} must be written with single quotes ('{value}'). Without them it is read as a host name.
invalid-keyword.invalid: {value} in {directive} isn't a CSP keyword, so it is ignored.

ignored.unsafe-inline: 'unsafe-inline' in {directive} is ignored because the rule also has a nonce or a hash. It only matters for very old browsers.
ignored.strict-dynamic: {value} in {directive} is ignored because of 'strict-dynamic': only scripts with the nonce or hash, and the scripts they load, run.

start.nonceQuestion: Can your site add a nonce to each page?

nonceExplain.simple: A nonce is a one-time code your server writes into each page and into its `<script>` tags. Only scripts carrying it run. Ask your developers: if they're not sure, choose **No**.
nonceExplain.developer: A fresh random value per response, sent in the policy and set as the `nonce` attribute of every `<script>`. With `'strict-dynamic'`, scripts loaded by a nonced script are trusted too, so tag managers keep working.
nonceExplain.security: A nonce with `'strict-dynamic'` resists the allowlist bypasses that affect host-based policies (JSONP, open redirects, script gadgets on allowed CDNs). It needs server-side rendering or an edge function to inject the value.

start.nonceHint: The strongest option: scripts run only if your page vouches for them.
start.allowlistHint: Scripts are trusted by where they come from. Simpler to run, easier to bypass.

site.question: Your pages
site.unsure: Not sure? Leave it unticked: the browser console will name what's blocked when you test the policy.
site.addressHint: Used to check what 'self' covers. Leave it empty if you prefer.

unrestricted.script: Your policy has no `script-src` or `default-src` yet: nothing restricts scripts, so every inline script already runs and these hashes change nothing. Start from a blank policy, or add one of those lines to your own.
unrestricted.style: Your policy has no `style-src` or `default-src` yet: nothing restricts styles, so every inline style already applies and these hashes change nothing. Start from a blank policy, or add one of those lines to your own.

script.simple: Paste each one below. Only these exact blocks will run: when one changes, its hash must be updated in the policy too.
script.technical: Each block is listed by its `'sha256-…'` hash. Once a hash is in `script-src`, browsers ignore `'unsafe-inline'` there: every inline script needs its hash, and `onclick="…"` attributes stop working.

style.simple: Paste each one below. Only these exact blocks will apply: when one changes, its hash must be updated in the policy too.
style.technical: Each block is listed by its `'sha256-…'` hash. Once a hash is in `style-src`, browsers ignore `'unsafe-inline'` there: every `<style>` block needs its hash, and `style="…"` attributes get `style-src-attr` of their own.

inline-scripts.label: Have code written directly in the page
inline-scripts.hint: <script> blocks with code inside, such as a tag snippet pasted into the page.
inline-scripts.detail: Inline <script> elements. Allowed with 'unsafe-inline', or with the nonce.

inline-handlers.label: Use onclick="…" attributes
inline-handlers.hint: Buttons or links with code in an attribute. Common in older sites and some themes.
inline-handlers.detail: Inline event handlers (script-src-attr). A nonce can't cover them: only 'unsafe-inline' or 'unsafe-hashes'.

eval.label: Run code built from text
eval.hint: Some older libraries and templates do this. Rare in modern sites.
eval.detail: eval(), new Function() or setTimeout with a string. Needs 'unsafe-eval'.

inline-styles.label: Have styles written directly in the page
inline-styles.hint: <style> blocks inside the page, common with page builders.
inline-styles.detail: Inline <style> elements. Allowed with 'unsafe-inline', or with the nonce.

style-attributes.label: Use style="…" attributes
style-attributes.hint: Elements styled one by one, common with page builders and rich-text content.

data-images.label: Show images written as data: addresses
data-images.hint: Small icons embedded in the code instead of loaded as files.
data-images.detail: data: URLs in img-src. Low risk for images.

summary.one: Value added for your site and tools: {count}. It's highlighted.
summary.other: Values added for your site and tools: {count}. They're highlighted.

review.intro: Highlighted values were added for your site or your tools.
review.fromStart: It was in your starting point.
review.copied: Copied from {directive} when this line was created, so nothing that worked before stops working.
review.nonce: `{placeholder}` stands for the value your server must generate: a new random one for **every page**, also set as the `nonce` attribute of your `<script>` tags. A fixed value gives no protection. [How to add it on your stack](/nonces#stacks-title).
review.useHashes: List your inline scripts by hash instead
review.reportOnly: Start with `Content-Security-Policy-Report-Only`: nothing is blocked, and the browser console lists what would be. When it stays quiet, switch to `Content-Security-Policy`. To have them sent to you instead of reading the console, [set up reporting](/reporting).
